summary: Defines a status message content type and XML namespace that tells an instant messaging user the other party is composing a message, for example typing or recording audio.

eli5.summary: It's the little "your friend is typing..." signal in chat apps.

questions: how does the typing indicator work in instant messaging
how long is the isComposing idle timeout
subtitle: How a chat client tells the other side that you are typing, recording audio or otherwise busy writing a reply.

tldr.problem: In a conversational instant messaging session, a quiet partner may have left, or may be about to answer. Without a signal, people assume the wrong thing and their messages cross on the wire.
tldr.mechanism: The composer's client sends a small XML status message, called isComposing, that says the user is active or idle. It travels in the same way as ordinary instant messages, and refresh and idle timers keep the state accurate.
tldr.outcome: The same indication works for text, audio and video, and the schema can be extended later. It is a Proposed Standard, and the RFC warns that it exposes fine-grained activity, so it needs careful confidentiality protection.

today: RFC 3994 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is still the definition of the isComposing indication.

sections.title: Why Tell Someone You Are Typing
sections.content:
Instant messaging (IM) is built from messages, but unlike email it is often a conversation, so the other person is waiting for an answer. If nothing arrives, a participant may wrongly assume that the partner has left, or that it is their own turn to type again. The result can be two messages crossing on the wire.

Several commercial IM systems already had an is-typing indication. RFC 3994 generalizes it into the isComposing status message. It can announce the composition of any media type, for example someone recording an audio or video clip, and it can be extended to carry other IM user states in the future.

The status messages are carried as XML and labeled with the application/im-iscomposing+xml content type. The RFC also records why it did not use presence (PIDF) instead: presence needs an explicit, periodic subscription, picking the right user agent is hard in page mode, and an in-band message is easier to translate across different IM systems.
sections.eli5: When you talk to a friend and they go quiet, you wonder if they left. A 'typing' sign tells you they are still there, getting a reply ready.

sections.title: The Composer's Two States and Timers
sections.content:
The RFC models a user as being in one of two states: idle or active. A user is idle by default, both before starting a message and after sending it. Only the user agent that is actually composing a content message generates status messages.

When the user starts composing, the state becomes active and an isComposing message with active in its <state> element goes to the recipient. There are two sender timers:

  • The active-state refresh interval says how often active messages are repeated. The composer picks it and announces it in the <refresh> element, in integer seconds. It SHOULD be no shorter than 60 seconds. A composer MAY skip refresh messages by leaving the element out, and then the receiver assumes idle after 120 seconds.
  • The idle time-out is how long the user can stop composing before an idle message is sent. Unless the user configures otherwise, it SHOULD default to 15 seconds.

If the content message is sent before the idle time-out expires, no idle message is needed, so usually only one status message is generated per content message. The rate is limited to one status message per refresh interval. The refresh mechanism exists for the case where the user logs off or the application crashes before the message is finished.
sections.eli5: Your app says 'I'm typing' when you start. If you stop for a short while it says 'I stopped', and if you keep going it repeats the news now and then so nobody gets fooled by an old sign.

sections.title: What the Receiver Does
sections.content:
The receiver watches the status messages to track the state of the content sender. If the latest active message carried a <refresh> value, that value is the time-out. Otherwise the time-out is 120 seconds.

The receiver moves from active back to idle in three cases:

  1. A status message with state idle arrives.
  2. A content message arrives.
  3. The refresh interval expires.

Receivers MUST be able to handle several consecutive active messages, whatever the refresh interval says. Recipients that implement the specification without extensions MUST treat any state token other than idle and active as idle, which keeps future extensions safe for old clients.
sections.eli5: The 'typing' sign goes away when your friend says 'I stopped', when their real message shows up, or when the sign has been on too long without being renewed.

sections.title: The isComposing Message
sections.content:
An isComposing document is XML that MUST be well formed and SHOULD be valid. It MUST be based on XML 1.0 and encoded in UTF-8. Its namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:im-iscomposing.

The root <isComposing> element has one mandatory child and three optional ones:

  • <state>: the composer state, idle or active.
  • <lastactive>: the absolute time when the user last added or edited content.
  • <contenttype>: the medium being composed, either a bare MIME type such as audio or text, or a type and subtype such as text/html. It is a hint to the human recipient, not a guarantee.
  • <refresh>: the interval after which an update is expected.

Extensions must use their own namespaces and be designed so receivers can safely ignore them. Adding elements to the namespace defined in this document is not permitted. The message MAY also be carried in CPIM messages, which is useful when a conference server relays it, because CPIM keeps the identity of the original composer.
sections.eli5: The message is a tiny form. It must say 'typing' or 'not typing', and it can also say what kind of thing you are making and how soon to expect more news.

sections.title: Session Mode and Page Mode
sections.content:
The status message works with both IM delivery styles, but session mode is the more natural fit. There it is sent as part of the messaging stream and its use is negotiated like any other media type in that stream. The RFC lists three benefits: it keeps proper ordering with the content messages, so an active indication does not show up after the message it describes; end-to-end security can be applied; and negotiation can switch the feature on or off at any time, even in one direction only.

In page mode the status message is the body of a page-mode message. In SIP-based IM, the composer MUST stop sending status messages if the receiver answers a MESSAGE request containing one with status code 415 (Unsupported Media Type). Delivery order is not assured, but SIP page mode allows only one unacknowledged message, so reordering is unlikely, though still possible when proxies are involved.
sections.eli5: Sending the sign inside the same chat as the messages keeps everything in order. If the other app says 'I do not understand these signs', your app stops sending them.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
An isComposing indication gives a fine-grained view of what the composer is doing, so it deserves careful confidentiality protection so that only the intended recipient receives it. Because the status messages travel over the IM protocol itself, every security consideration of that protocol also applies.

There are privacy risks when status messages are sent before a conversation exists, since one may be sent even if the user later abandons the message. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS that in page mode the indication is sent only while composing a reply to an earlier message. It does not say how to detect that, but suggests elapsed time or user interface behavior as hints.
sections.eli5: A typing sign tells people a lot about what you are doing, so only the person you are talking to should see it, and it should not be sent to strangers.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers three things: the media type application/im-iscomposing+xml (a specialization of application/xml, with an optional charset parameter that defaults to UTF-8), the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:im-iscomposing, and the schema, whose XML is the sole content of Section 6.1.

The media type registration marks its intended usage as LIMITED USE, names instant messaging systems as the applications that use it, and repeats that the information about current user activity may be private.
sections.eli5: The authors put the new message type and its name on the official list, so nobody else picks the same name for something different.
